raw_case_text:
A 54 years old male Ugandan presented to Kenyatta National Hospital, a major referral tertiary hospital, in Kenya. He had initially reported with headache and joint pain to a local health facility in Uganda and was diagnosed to have severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria infection, and thereafter treatment with intravenous quinine commenced.
Treatment at the facility had been responsive; however two days after the onset, the patient started experiencing episodes of headache, pain, numbness, coldness, and swelling of the extremities. This was followed by darkening of the digits of his toes and hands, which gradually progressed proximally.
On presentation at out institution, he was conscious, alert, oriented, but lethargic and unable to walk. He was a non-smoker and non-alcoholic, and had no history of diabetes, hypertension or any angiopathies. He however had a history of numerous episodes of malaria bouts and a family history of hypertension with his father having succumbed to a stroke.
On physical examination, apart from fever, abdominal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems were normal. Jaundice, pallor and cyanosis were absent. A right low paramedian scar was noted secondary to appendicectomy conducted in the year 1995. On local examination, the overlying skin cold, dry, wrinkled, and was darkened with a clear line of proximal demarcation (Figure 1). Pain was present in the regions proximal to the discolouration, and absent in the distal regions.
Investigations tested negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL on ELISA. Urea, Electrolyte and creatinine tests were normal. Clotting profile showed a prolonged Prothrombin time of 19sec, Prothrombin time index of 74%, and an INR of 1.36. A haemogram showed macrocytic normochromic anaemia (Hb 9.03 g/dL, MCV 89.9fL, MCH 29.5pg, MCHC 27.2g/dL), Hct 33.2%, RBC 3.69x1012/L. WBC 4.39x109, Neutrophils 2.11x109 (48.2%), Lymphocytes 1.73x109 (39.5%), Monocytes 0.314x109 (7.16%), Eosinophils 0.193x109 (4.4%), Basophils 0.035x109 (0.796%).
An echocardiogram was normal except for type 1 left ventricular dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation. The Dorsalis pedis pulses showed absence of blood flow, and a diagnosis of Symmetrical peripheral gangrene was made. Management was initiated with clopidogrel, Acetylsalicylic Acid, and Atorvastatin, and quad-amputation recommended. Time was allowed for marginalization of the gangrene, which was noted two months later. Meanwhile fresh frozen plasma was regularly administered to counter suspected thrombophilia.
Following satisfactory marginalization of the gangrene, the patient underwent surgical excision of the necrotic tissue. This involved transmetatarsal amputation of both feet and ray amputation of the hands. The wounds healed well thereafter facilitated by vacuum dressing at -7.5mmHg over one month. He was then referred to plastic surgeons for prosthesis.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old male presenting with numbness, coldness, severe pain, and progressive symmetric blackening of the fingers and toes.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 54-year-old male initially presented to a health facility in Uganda with headache and arthralgias and was treated for a severe febrile illness. Two days following treatment initiation, he developed headache, intense limb pain, numbness, coldness, and swelling of his distal extremities, rapidly followed by symmetrical darkening of the digits of his feet and hands that progressed proximally. He was transferred to a tertiary referral hospital in Nairobi, Kenya, unable to walk due to dry gangrene.
subjective.past_medical_history: Ugandan male; history of numerous prior bouts of malaria. Non-smoker, non-drinker. No history of diabetes mellitus, hypertension, or angiopathies. Family history of hypertension and fatal stroke in father. Surgical history: appendectomy in 1995. Completed IV quinine prior to transfer.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for headache, arthralgia, severe limb pain proximal to discoloration, distal numbness, coldness, and swelling. Negative for chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, or bowel/bladder dysfunction. Medications: completed course of IV quinine. Allergies: null.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious, alert, oriented, but lethargic and unable to walk. Febrile. Jaundice, pallor, and cyanosis were absent. Abdominal, cardiovascular, respiratory, and neurological systems were normal. Abdomen showed a right lower paramedian appendectomy scar. Extremity examination: skin of bilateral distal hands and feet was cold, dry, wrinkled, and blackened with a clear line of proximal demarcation. Severe tenderness present proximal to demarcation; distal areas were insensate. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses were absent.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemogram: macrocytic normochromic anemia with hemoglobin 9.03 g/dL, MCV 89.9 fL, MCH 29.5 pg, MCHC 27.2 g/dL, hematocrit 33.2%, red blood cells 3.69 x 10^12/L; leukocytes 4.39 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 48.2%, lymphocytes 39.5%, monocytes 7.16%, eosinophils 4.4%, basophils 0.8%). Coagulation profile: prothrombin time 19 sec, prothrombin time index 74%, INR 1.36. Urea, electrolytes, and creatinine: normal. Serology: negative for HIV, HBV, HCV, and VDRL on ELISA.
objective.advanced_workup: Transthoracic echocardiogram: type 1 left ventricular diastolic dysfunction and mild tricuspid regurgitation, without intracardiac vegetations or thrombi. Peripheral vascular Doppler: confirmed complete absence of blood flow in bilateral dorsalis pedis arteries.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Symmetrical peripheral gangrene (purpura fulminans / post-infectious microvascular thrombosis of all four extremities) complicating severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.
Diagnostic confirmation: Documented severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria initially treated with intravenous quinine; negative serologic screening for HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and syphilis; echocardiography excluding central embolic sources; Doppler demonstrating peripheral arterial flow arrest.
Treatment & Outcome: Managed medically with clopidogrel, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), atorvastatin, and regular administration of fresh frozen plasma to counteract suspected hypercoagulability/thrombophilia. Following 2 months of conservative observation to allow complete ischemic demarcation, he underwent surgical amputation comprising bilateral transmetatarsal amputations of the feet and ray amputations of both hands. Wounds were managed with negative-pressure vacuum dressings at -7.5 mmHg for 1 month, achieving primary healing, and he was referred for plastic surgical prosthesis.
